name: Elamipretide
used_for: FDA-approved under accelerated approval (NDA 215244, Forzinity, approval action dated September 2025) to improve muscle strength in adults and children with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg. The label says continued approval may depend on a confirmatory trial. It is not approved for aging, longevity, heart failure, mitochondrial myopathy or any other use; the large primary mitochondrial myopathy trial missed its main endpoints.

entries.text: Label: 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, at the same time each day.
entries.population: Patients with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg

entries.text: Label: 20 mg subcutaneously once daily for adults with eGFR below 30 mL/min who are not on dialysis; the label says there is insufficient information to recommend a dose for adults on dialysis.
entries.population: Adults with Barth syndrome and severe renal impairment

side_effects.text: Injection site reactions were the main adverse reactions in the label's trial data (12 patients, versus placebo): erythema 100% (placebo 25%), pain 75% (42%), induration 67% (17%), pruritus 67% (17%), bruising 25% (0%) and urticaria 25% (0%).
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: The label warns of hypersensitivity reactions (rash, dermatitis, respiratory symptoms) and says to discontinue if severe reactions occur.
side_effects.label: research

side_effects.text: The label warns of benzyl alcohol toxicity in neonates (metabolic acidosis, gasping syndrome); the product is not approved for neonates.

internet_claims.claim: Empire Medical Training, a CME course provider, describes SS-31 as the first mitochondrial-targeted peptide with FDA approval, but only for Barth syndrome, calls longevity uses off-label and investigational, and says the human trial record is mixed, with a heart failure study negative on its primary endpoint.

Forge Biology, an educational site, says SS-31 improves ATP production and reduces oxidative stress, and may support endurance, heart health and longevity, mentioning human trials without giving citations; most of the evidence it discusses appears to be animal work.

research.summary: FDA-approved DailyMed prescribing information for Forzinity (elamipretide) injection, published 12 December 2025.
research.finding: Indicated under accelerated approval to improve muscle strength in Barth syndrome (30 kg or more). The label says the randomized trial in 12 patients was not superior to placebo on its primary endpoints (6-minute walk and fatigue); knee muscle strength rose in the open-label extension, not the randomized period. Most common adverse reactions are injection site reactions; the label carries a benzyl alcohol warning for neonates.

research.summary: TAZPOWER: 28-week randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial in Barth syndrome followed by a 168-week open-label extension of elamipretide 40 mg daily (Genet Med; NCT03098797).
research.finding: Ten patients entered the extension; 8 reached week 168. Six-minute walk and fatigue scores improved versus extension baseline, with injection site reactions the main adverse event. Uncontrolled extension in very few patients.

research.summary: MMPOWER-3: 24-week randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of elamipretide 40 mg daily in 218 adults with primary mitochondrial myopathy (Neurology; NCT03323749).
research.finding: The trial did not meet either primary endpoint: 6-minute walk difference -3.2 m (p=0.69) and no significant difference in fatigue score. The drug was generally well tolerated.

research.summary: MMPOWER-2: randomized crossover trial of elamipretide 40 mg daily for 4 weeks versus placebo in 30 adults with primary mitochondrial myopathy (J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle; NCT02805790).
research.finding: The 6-minute walk improved by 19.8 m but was not statistically significant (p=0.083); fatigue scores favored elamipretide. Injection site reactions occurred in 80%. Small, short trial.

research.summary: FDA warning letter dated 24 August 2026 to Royal Peptides LLC.
research.finding: The letter lists SS-31 (Elamipretide), among other peptides, as unapproved new drugs sold with research-use-only labels despite evidence of intended human use.

dose.summary: The FDA label (Forzinity, approved for Barth syndrome) gives 40 mg under the skin once daily, and 20 mg for adults with severe kidney impairment not on dialysis. Online sources describe much lower doses, from 0.5 to 20 mg a day, for uses that have not been studied in healthy adults.

cycle_length.summary: The label describes continuous daily use and names no breaks. The randomized trial lasted 12 weeks, and a small uncontrolled extension followed 8 patients to week 168. Online cycles of 4 to 8 weeks on then weeks off are untested and differ from the label. No withdrawal data were found.

mechanism.summary: The label says elamipretide binds cardiolipin, a fat found in the inner membrane of mitochondria (the cell's energy units), and improves their shape and function. How this leads to better muscle strength in people is not established.

items.text: Label section 12.1: Forzinity is a mitochondrial cardiolipin binder that localizes to the inner mitochondrial membrane and improves mitochondrial morphology and function.

best_documented_effect.summary: The 12-patient Barth syndrome trial was not better than placebo on its main endpoints (6-minute walk and fatigue). Knee strength rose only in the uncontrolled extension. The large mitochondrial myopathy trial also missed its main endpoints.

items.text: Label: in a randomized trial of 12 patients with Barth syndrome, elamipretide was not superior to placebo on 6-minute walk or fatigue. Median knee strength change was 4 newtons versus -5 on placebo at week 12 (baseline 124 N), and 63 newtons at week 168 in the 8 extension patients.
